w: Raised around 100 AD, just after Rome's Colosseum, this amphitheatre once held 24,000 spectators across 34 tiers for gladiator fights and beast hunts. Medieval Nimes turned it into a fortress, then a walled town, before 19th-century restorers cleared the houses back out. Bullfights and concerts fill it now.
s: A Roman arena still packing crowds two millennia on
_facts: Roman amphitheatre built around 100 AD, one of the best-preserved in the world, held 24,000 spectators over 34 tiers
used for gladiator battles and animal hunts in Roman times; converted to a fortress then a walled town in the medieval era
19th-century restoration removed houses built inside; today hosts annual bullfights during the Feria de Nimes plus reenactments and concerts

w: Norman Foster beat Frank Gehry and Jean Nouvel to design this glass-and-steel museum, deliberately half-sunk into the ground so it wouldn't upstage the 2,000-year-old Roman temple it faces. Opened in 1993, it holds contemporary art, the city library, and a cinema in its buried lower floors.
s: Norman Foster's answer to a Roman temple
_facts: contemporary art museum and municipal library facing the Maison Carree, a Roman temple
1984 design competition included Frank Gehry, Jean Nouvel and Cesar Pelli; Norman Foster's design was chosen
opened May 1993; nine-storey structure half-sunk into the ground to keep a low profile, with archival storage and a cinema in the lower levels

w: Despite the name, there's no real evidence this Roman ruin was ever dedicated to Diana -- its basilica-like layout suggests a library instead. A medieval monastery moved in and kept it standing; 18th-century painters like Hubert Robert kept sketching it. Excavated from the Jardins de la Fontaine in 1745.
s: A 'temple' that was probably never Diana's
_facts: 1st-century Roman building built under Augustus, near the Fontaine spring, part of an Augusteum sanctuary
basilica-like floor plan argues against a dedication to Diana; no evidence for the name; may have been a library
survived as a medieval monastery; excavated in 1745 during garden works, painted by Hubert Robert, monument historique since 1840

w: Built, it's believed, on the foundations of a lost Temple of Augustus, this part-Romanesque, part-Gothic cathedral has been the seat of the Bishops of Nimes since the Middle Ages. Dedicated to the Virgin and to the local Saint Castor of Apt, and a historical monument since 1906.
s: A cathedral raised over a vanished Roman temple
_facts: Roman Catholic cathedral dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Castor of Apt, seat of the Bishops of Nimes
believed to stand on the site of the former Temple of Augustus
partly Romanesque, partly Gothic; classified a historical monument in 1906

w: One of the youngest additions to Nimes' museum scene, this archaeology museum opened on 2 June 2018 -- a sleek modern showcase for a city that has been sitting on Roman remains for two thousand years, built to give them a proper stage at last.
s: Nimes' newest window onto its Roman past
